{{Short description|Data analysis method}}
[[File:L1-PCA.png|thumb|right| L1-PCA compared with PCA. Nominal data (blue points); outlier (red point); PC (black line); L1-PC (red line); nominal maximum-variance line (dotted line).]]

'''L1-norm principal component analysis (L1-PCA)''' is a general method for multivariate data analysis.<ref name="mark2014">{{cite journal|last1=Markopoulos|first1=Panos P.|last2=Karystinos|first2=George N.|last3=Pados|first3=Dimitris A.|title=Optimal Algorithms for L1-subspace Signal Processing|journal=IEEE Transactions on Signal Processing|date=October 2014|volume=62|issue=19|pages=5046–5058|doi=10.1109/TSP.2014.2338077|arxiv=1405.6785|bibcode=2014ITSP...62.5046M|s2cid=1494171}}</ref>
L1-PCA is often preferred over standard L2-norm [[principal component analysis]] (PCA) when the analyzed data may contain [[Outlier|outliers]] (faulty values or corruptions), as it is believed to be [[Robust statistics|robust]].<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Barrodale|first1=I.|title=L1 Approximation and the Analysis of Data|journal=Applied Statistics|date=1968|volume=17|issue=1|pages=51–57|doi=10.2307/2985267|jstor=2985267}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|last1=Barnett|first1=Vic|last2=Lewis|first2=Toby|title=Outliers in statistical data|date=1994|publisher=Wiley|location=Chichester [u.a.]|isbn=978-0471930945|edition=3.}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|last1=Kanade|first1=T.|last2=Ke|first2=Qifa|title=2005 IEEE Computer Society Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR'05) |chapter=Robust L₁ Norm Factorization in the Presence of Outliers and Missing Data by Alternative Convex Programming |volume=1|pages=739–746|date=June 2005|doi=10.1109/CVPR.2005.309|publisher=IEEE|isbn=978-0-7695-2372-9|citeseerx=10.1.1.63.4605|s2cid=17144854}}</ref>

Both L1-PCA and standard PCA seek a collection of [[Orthogonality|orthogonal]] directions (principal components) that define a [[Linear subspace|subspace]] wherein data representation is maximized according to the selected criterion.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Jolliffe|first1=I.T.|title=Principal component analysis|date=2004|publisher=Springer|location=New York|isbn=978-0387954424|edition=2nd|url-access=registration|url=https://archive.org/details/principalcompone00joll_0}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|last1=Bishop|first1=Christopher M.|title=Pattern recognition and machine learning|date=2007|publisher=Springer|location=New York|isbn=978-0-387-31073-2|edition=Corr. printing.}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last1=Pearson|first1=Karl|title=On Lines and Planes of Closest Fit to Systems of Points in Space|journal=The London, Edinburgh, and Dublin Philosophical Magazine and Journal of Science|date=8 June 2010|volume=2|issue=11|pages=559–572|doi=10.1080/14786440109462720|s2cid=125037489 |url=https://zenodo.org/record/1430636}}</ref>
Standard PCA quantifies data representation as the aggregate of the [[Norm (mathematics)#Euclidean_norm|L2-norm]] of the data point [[Projection_(linear_algebra)|projections]] into the subspace, or equivalently the aggregate [[Euclidean distance]] of the original points from their subspace-projected representations.
L1-PCA uses instead the aggregate of the L1-norm of the data point projections into the subspace.<ref name="mark2017">{{cite journal|last1=Markopoulos|first1=Panos P.|last2=Kundu|first2=Sandipan|last3=Chamadia|first3=Shubham|last4=Pados|first4=Dimitris A.|title=Efficient L1-Norm Principal-Component Analysis via Bit Flipping|journal=IEEE Transactions on Signal Processing|date=15 August 2017|volume=65|issue=16|pages=4252–4264|doi=10.1109/TSP.2017.2708023|arxiv=1610.01959|bibcode=2017ITSP...65.4252M|s2cid=7931130}}</ref> In PCA and L1-PCA, the number of principal components (PCs) is lower than the [[Rank (linear algebra)|rank]] of the analyzed matrix, which coincides with the dimensionality of the space defined by the original data points.
Therefore, PCA or L1-PCA are commonly employed for [[dimensionality reduction]] for the purpose of data denoising or compression.
Among the advantages of standard PCA that contributed to its high popularity are [[Computational complexity|low-cost]] computational implementation by means of [[singular-value decomposition]] (SVD)<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Golub|first1=Gene H.|title=Some Modified Matrix Eigenvalue Problems|journal=SIAM Review|date=April 1973|volume=15|issue=2|pages=318–334|doi=10.1137/1015032|citeseerx=10.1.1.454.9868}}</ref> and statistical optimality when the data set is generated by a true [[Multivariate normal distribution|multivariate normal]] data source.

However, in modern big data sets, data often include corrupted, faulty points, commonly referred to as outliers.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Barnett|first1=Vic|last2=Lewis|first2=Toby|title=Outliers in statistical data|date=1994|publisher=Wiley|location=Chichester [u.a.]|isbn=978-0471930945|edition=3.}}</ref>
Standard PCA is known to be sensitive to outliers, even when they appear as a small fraction of the processed data.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Candès|first1=Emmanuel J.|last2=Li|first2=Xiaodong|last3=Ma|first3=Yi|last4=Wright|first4=John|title=Robust principal component analysis?|journal=Journal of the ACM|date=1 May 2011|volume=58|issue=3|pages=1–37|doi=10.1145/1970392.1970395|arxiv=0912.3599|s2cid=7128002}}</ref>
The reason is that the L2-norm formulation of L2-PCA places squared emphasis on the magnitude of each coordinate of each data point, ultimately overemphasizing peripheral points, such as outliers. 
On the other hand, following an L1-norm formulation, L1-PCA places linear emphasis on the coordinates of each data point, effectively restraining outliers.<ref name="kwak2008">{{cite journal|last1=Kwak|first1=N.|title=Principal Component Analysis Based on L1-Norm Maximization|journal=IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence|date=September 2008|volume=30|issue=9|pages=1672–1680|doi=10.1109/TPAMI.2008.114|pmid=18617723|citeseerx=10.1.1.333.1176|s2cid=11882870}}</ref>

== Formulation ==
Consider any [[Matrix (mathematics)|matrix]] <math>\mathbf X = [\mathbf x_1, \mathbf x_2, \ldots, \mathbf x_N] \in \mathbb R^{D \times N}</math> consisting of <math>N</math> <math>D</math>-dimensional data points. Define <math>r=rank(\mathbf X)</math>. For integer <math>K</math> such that <math>1 \leq K < r</math>, L1-PCA is formulated as:<ref name="mark2014" />

{{NumBlk|:|
<math>
\begin{align}
&\underset{\mathbf Q=[\mathbf q_1, \mathbf q_2, \ldots, \mathbf q_K] \in \mathbb R^{D \times K}}{\max}~~\| \mathbf X^\top \mathbf Q\|_1\\
&\text{subject to}~~ \mathbf Q^\top \mathbf Q=\mathbf I_K.
\end{align}
</math>
|{{EquationRef|1}}}}

For <math>K=1</math>, ({{EquationNote|1}}) simplifies to finding the L1-norm principal component (L1-PC) of <math>\mathbf X</math> by
{{NumBlk|:|
<math>
\begin{align}
&\underset{\mathbf q \in \mathbb R^{D \times 1}}{\max}~~\| \mathbf X^\top \mathbf q\|_1\\
&\text{subject to}~~ \| \mathbf q\|_2 =1.
\end{align}
</math>
|{{EquationRef|2}}}}

In ({{EquationNote|1}})-({{EquationNote|2}}), [[Norm (mathematics)|L1-norm]] <math>\| \cdot \|_1</math> returns the sum of the absolute entries of its argument and L2-norm <math>\| \cdot \|_2</math> returns the sum of the squared entries of its argument. If one substitutes <math>\| \cdot \|_1</math> in ({{EquationNote|2}}) by the [[Matrix norm#Frobenius norm|Frobenius]]/L2-norm <math>\| \cdot \|_F</math>, then the problem becomes standard PCA and it is solved by the matrix  <math>\mathbf Q</math> that contains the <math>K</math> dominant singular vectors of <math>\mathbf X</math> (i.e., the singular vectors that correspond to the <math>K</math> highest [[Singular value|singular values]]).

The maximization metric in ({{EquationNote|2}}) can be expanded as 
{{NumBlk|:|
<math>\| \mathbf X^\top \mathbf Q\|_1=\sum_{k=1}^K \sum_{n=1}^N |\mathbf x_n^\top \mathbf q_k|.
</math>
|{{EquationRef|3}}}}

== Solution ==

For any matrix <math>\mathbf A \in \mathbb R^{m \times n}</math> with <math>m \geq n</math>, define <math>\Phi(\mathbf A)</math> as the nearest (in the L2-norm sense) matrix to <math>\mathbf A</math> that has orthonormal columns. That is, define
{{NumBlk|:|
<math>
\begin{align}
\Phi(\mathbf A) = & \underset{\mathbf Q \in \mathbb R^{m \times n}}{\text{argmin}}~~\| \mathbf A - \mathbf Q\|_F\\
&\text{subject to}~~ \mathbf Q^\top \mathbf Q=\mathbf I_n.
\end{align}
</math>
|{{EquationRef|4}}}}
Procrustes Theorem<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Eldén|first1=Lars|last2=Park|first2=Haesun|title=A Procrustes problem on the Stiefel manifold|journal=Numerische Mathematik|date=1 June 1999|volume=82|issue=4|pages=599–619|doi=10.1007/s002110050432|citeseerx=10.1.1.54.3580|s2cid=206895591}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last1=Schönemann|first1=Peter H.|title=A generalized solution of the orthogonal procrustes problem|journal=Psychometrika|date=March 1966|volume=31|issue=1|pages=1–10|doi=10.1007/BF02289451|hdl=10338.dmlcz/103138|s2cid=121676935|hdl-access=free}}</ref> states that if <math>\mathbf A</math> has SVD <math>\mathbf U_{m \times n} \boldsymbol \Sigma_{n \times n} \mathbf V_{n \times n}^\top</math>, then 
<math>\Phi(\mathbf A)=\mathbf U \mathbf V^\top </math>.

Markopoulos, Karystinos, and Pados<ref name="mark2014" /> showed that, if <math>\mathbf B_{\text{BNM}}</math> is the exact solution to the binary nuclear-norm maximization (BNM) problem 
{{NumBlk|:|
<math>
\begin{align}
\underset{\mathbf B \in \{ \pm 1\}^{N \times K}}{\text{max}}~~\| \mathbf X \mathbf B\|_*^2,
\end{align}
</math>
|{{EquationRef|5}}}}
then 
{{NumBlk|:|
<math>
\begin{align}
\mathbf Q_{\text{L1}} = \Phi(\mathbf X\mathbf B_{\text{BNM}})
\end{align}
</math>
|{{EquationRef|6}}}}
is the exact solution to L1-PCA in ({{EquationNote|2}}). The [[Matrix norm|nuclear-norm]] <math>\| \cdot \|_*</math> in ({{EquationNote|2}}) returns the summation of the singular values of its matrix argument and can be calculated by means of standard SVD. Moreover, it holds that, given the solution to L1-PCA, <math>\mathbf Q_{\text{L1}}</math>, the solution to BNM can be obtained as 
{{NumBlk|:|
<math>
\begin{align}
\mathbf B_{\text{BNM}} = \text{sgn}(\mathbf X^\top \mathbf Q_{\text{L1}}) 
\end{align}
</math>
|{{EquationRef|7}}}}
where <math>\text{sgn}(\cdot)</math> returns the <math>\{\pm 1\}</math>-sign matrix of its matrix argument (with no loss of generality, we can consider <math>\text{sgn}(0)=1</math>). In addition, it follows that <math> \| \mathbf X^\top \mathbf Q_{\text{L1}}\|_1 = \| \mathbf X \mathbf B_{\text{BNM}}\|_*</math>. BNM in ({{EquationNote|5}})  is a [[Combinatorics|combinatorial]] problem over antipodal binary variables. Therefore, its exact solution can be found through exhaustive evaluation of all <math>2^{NK}</math> elements of its feasibility set, with [[Computational complexity|asymptotic cost]] <math>\mathcal O(2^{NK})</math>. Therefore, L1-PCA can also be solved, through BNM, with cost <math>\mathcal O(2^{NK})</math> (exponential in the product of the number of data points with the number of the sought-after components). It turns out that L1-PCA can be solved optimally (exactly) with polynomial complexity in <math>N</math> for fixed data dimension <math>D</math>'', <math>\mathcal{O}(N^{rK-K+1})</math>''.<ref name="mark2014" />

For the special case of <math>K=1</math> (single L1-PC of <math>\mathbf X</math>), BNM takes the binary-quadratic-maximization (BQM) form 
{{NumBlk|:|
<math>
\begin{align}
& \underset{\mathbf b \in \{ \pm 1\}^{N \times 1}}{\text{max}}~~ \mathbf b^\top \mathbf X^\top \mathbf X \mathbf b.
\end{align}
</math>
|{{EquationRef|8}}}}
The transition from ({{EquationNote|5}})  to ({{EquationNote|8}}) for <math>K=1</math> holds true, since the unique singular value of <math>\mathbf X \mathbf b</math> is equal to <math>\| \mathbf X \mathbf b\|_2 = \sqrt{\mathbf b^\top \mathbf X^\top \mathbf X \mathbf b}</math>, for every <math>\mathbf b </math>. Then, if  <math>\mathbf b_{\text{BNM}}</math> is the solution to BQM in ({{EquationNote|7}}), it holds that 
{{NumBlk|:|
<math>
\begin{align}
\mathbf q_{\text{L1}} = \Phi(\mathbf X \mathbf b_{\text{BNM}}) = \frac{\mathbf X \mathbf b_{\text{BNM}}}{\| \mathbf X \mathbf b_{\text{BNM}}\|_2} 
\end{align}
</math>
|{{EquationRef|9}}}}
is the exact L1-PC of <math>\mathbf X</math>, as defined in ({{EquationNote|1}}). In addition, it holds that <math>\mathbf b_{\text{BNM}} = \text{sgn}(\mathbf X^\top \mathbf q_{\text{L1}})</math> and <math> \| \mathbf X^\top \mathbf q_{\text{L1}}\|_1 = \| \mathbf X \mathbf b_{\text{BNM}}\|_2</math>.

== Algorithms ==
=== Exact solution of exponential complexity ===

As shown above, the exact solution to L1-PCA can be obtained by the following two-step process: 
 1. Solve the problem in ({{EquationNote|5}}) to obtain <math>\mathbf B_{\text{BNM}}</math>.
 2. Apply SVD on <math>\mathbf X\mathbf B_{\text{BNM}}</math> to obtain <math>\mathbf Q_{\text{L1}}</math>.

BNM in ({{EquationNote|5}}) can be solved by exhaustive search over the domain of '''<math>\mathbf B</math>''' with cost <math>\mathcal{O}(2^{NK})</math>. 

=== Exact solution of polynomial complexity ===
Also, L1-PCA can be solved optimally with cost <math>\mathcal{O}(N^{rK-K+1})</math>, when <math>r=rank(\mathbf X)</math> is constant with respect to <math>N</math> (always true for finite data dimension <math>D</math>).<ref name="mark2014" /><ref>{{cite book|last1=Markopoulos|first1=PP|last2=Kundu|first2=S|last3=Chamadia|first3=S|last4=Tsagkarakis|first4=N|last5=Pados|first5=DA|title=Advances in Principal Component Analysis |chapter=Outlier-Resistant Data Processing with L1-Norm Principal Component Analysis |date=2018|issue=Springer, Singapore|pages=121–135|doi=10.1007/978-981-10-6704-4_6|isbn=978-981-10-6703-7}}</ref>

=== Approximate efficient solvers ===

In 2008, Kwak<ref name="kwak2008" /> proposed an iterative algorithm for the approximate solution of L1-PCA for <math>K=1</math>. This iterative method was later generalized for <math>K>1</math> components.<ref name="nie2011">{{cite journal|last1=Nie|first1=F|last2=Huang|first2=H|last3=Ding|first3=C|last4=Luo|first4=Dijun|last5=Wang|first5=H|title=Robust principal component analysis with non-greedy l1-norm maximization|journal=22nd International Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence|date=July 2011|pages=1433–1438}}</ref> Another approximate efficient solver was proposed by McCoy and Tropp<ref>{{cite journal|last1=McCoy|first1=Michael|last2=Tropp|first2=Joel A.|date=2011|title=Two proposals for robust PCA using semidefinite programming|journal=Electronic Journal of Statistics|volume=5|pages=1123–1160|doi=10.1214/11-EJS636|arxiv=1012.1086|s2cid=14102421}}</ref> by means of semi-definite programming (SDP). Most recently, L1-PCA (and BNM in ({{EquationNote|5}})) were solved efficiently by means of bit-flipping iterations (L1-BF algorithm).<ref name="mark2017" />

==== L1-BF algorithm ====

  1  '''function''' L1BF(<math>\mathbf X</math>, <math>K</math>):
  2      Initialize <math>\mathbf B^{(0)} \in \{\pm 1\}^{N \times K}</math> and <math>\mathcal L \leftarrow \{1,2,\ldots, NK\}</math>
  3      Set <math>t \leftarrow 0</math> and <math>\omega \leftarrow \| \mathbf X \mathbf B^{(0)} \|_*</math>
  4      Until termination (or <math>T</math> iterations)
  5          <math>\mathbf B \leftarrow \mathbf B^{(t)}</math>, <math>t' \leftarrow t</math>
  6          For <math>x \in \mathcal L</math>
  7              <math>k \leftarrow \lceil \frac{x}{N} \rceil</math>, <math>n \leftarrow x-N(k-1)</math>
  8              <math>[\mathbf B]_{n,k} \leftarrow - [\mathbf B]_{n,k}</math>                ''// flip bit''
  9              <math>a(n,k) \leftarrow \| \mathbf X \mathbf B \|_*</math>               ''// calculated by SVD or faster (see<ref name="mark2017" />)''
 10              if <math>a(n,k)>\omega</math>
 11                  <math>\mathbf B^{(t)} \leftarrow  \mathbf B</math>, <math>t' \leftarrow t+1</math>
 12                  <math>\omega \leftarrow  a(n,k)</math>
 13              end
 14              if <math>t'=t</math>                    ''// no bit was flipped''
 15                  if <math>\mathcal L = \{1,2, \ldots, NK\}</math>
 16                      terminate
 17                  else
 18                      <math>\mathcal L \leftarrow \{1,2, \ldots, NK\}</math>

The computational cost of L1-BF is <math>\mathcal O (ND min\{N,D\} + N^2K^2(K^2 + r))</math>.<ref name="mark2017"/>

== Complex data ==

L1-PCA has also been generalized to process [[Complex number|complex]] data. For complex L1-PCA, two efficient algorithms were proposed in 2018.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Tsagkarakis|first1=Nicholas|last2=Markopoulos|first2=Panos P.|last3=Sklivanitis|first3=George|last4=Pados|first4=Dimitris A.|title=L1-Norm Principal-Component Analysis of Complex Data|journal=IEEE Transactions on Signal Processing|date=15 June 2018|volume=66|issue=12|pages=3256–3267|doi=10.1109/TSP.2018.2821641|arxiv=1708.01249|bibcode=2018ITSP...66.3256T|s2cid=21011653}}</ref>

== Tensor data ==

L1-PCA has also been extended for the analysis of [[tensor]] data, in the form of L1-Tucker, the L1-norm robust analogous of standard [[Tucker decomposition]].<ref name="l1tucker">{{cite journal|last1=Chachlakis|first1=Dimitris G.|last2=Prater-Bennette|first2=Ashley|last3=Markopoulos|first3=Panos P.|title=L1-norm Tucker Tensor Decomposition|journal=IEEE Access|date=22 November 2019|volume=7|pages=178454–178465|doi=10.1109/ACCESS.2019.2955134|arxiv=1904.06455|doi-access=free}}</ref> Two algorithms for the solution of L1-Tucker are L1-HOSVD and L1-HOOI.<ref name="l1tucker"/><ref name="l1tucker2">{{cite book|last1=Markopoulos|first1=Panos P.|last2=Chachlakis|first2=Dimitris G.|last3=Prater-Bennette|first3=Ashley|title=2018 IEEE Global Conference on Signal and Information Processing (GlobalSIP) |chapter=L1-Norm Higher-Order Singular-Value Decomposition |date=21 February 2019|pages=1353–1357|doi=10.1109/GlobalSIP.2018.8646385|isbn=978-1-7281-1295-4|s2cid=67874182}}</ref><ref name="l1tucker3">{{cite journal|last1=Markopoulos|first1=Panos P.|last2=Chachlakis|first2=Dimitris G.|last3=Papalexakis|first3=Evangelos|title=The Exact Solution to Rank-1 L1-Norm TUCKER2 Decomposition
|journal=IEEE Signal Processing Letters|volume=25|issue=4|date=April 2018|pages=511–515|doi=10.1109/LSP.2018.2790901|arxiv=1710.11306|bibcode=2018ISPL...25..511M|s2cid=3693326}}</ref>
